t: Pizza With 3n Slices — Circular House Robber with a Budget
o:
## Understanding the problem

Each turn you take one slice, then your two friends take the immediate neighbors on both sides. Since every round removes exactly 3 slices and there are 3n slices, **you take exactly n slices**. Crucially, after you pick slice i, its two neighbors are removed by friends, so the slices you end up keeping are always **non-adjacent in the original circular arrangement**. Conversely, any set of n pairwise non-adjacent slices is achievable (pick them in any order). So the problem reduces to: *choose exactly n elements from a circular array, no two adjacent, maximizing their sum*.

For `[1,2,3,4,5,6]` we choose {4,6} (sum 10); choosing 5 instead of 6 would block 4 and 6, giving at most 9. For `[8,9,8,6,1,1]` choosing 9 forces both 8s away, so the best is {8,8} = 16 — this shows a naive "always take the biggest" greedy fails.

With length up to 500 (n up to ~167), an exponential search over subsets is too slow, but a polynomial DP over positions and count of picks fits easily.
k: You must take exactly n slices, and they are always pairwise non-adjacent in the circular array — this is 'House Robber' plus an exact-count constraint.
Handle circularity by solving the problem twice on the linearized array: once excluding the first slice, once excluding the last slice.
A greedy by largest value fails (see example 2), because taking a big slice can destroy two other good picks.

a.i: Try every valid choice recursively: at each step pick some remaining slice, remove it and its neighbors, recurse until n picks are made. This directly mirrors the game rules and confirms the reduction to non-adjacent selection, but explores exponentially many combinations, so it only works for tiny inputs.
s: Recursively enumerate all ways to make n picks from the current list of remaining slices.
When picking index i, delete i-1, i, i+1 (circularly) from the working list.
Track the best total over all branches; prune when fewer than 3*(remaining picks) - 2 slices remain.
a.t: Exponential — roughly C(3n, n) branches, each doing O(n) list work; only viable for very small inputs.
a.sp: O(n) recursion depth plus temporary lists per call.

a.n: Approach 2: Linear DP (House Robber with exact count), solved twice for circularity
a.i: On a *linear* array, define dp[i][j] = max sum picking j non-adjacent slices among the first i slices. Either slice i is taken (dp[i-2][j-1] + v[i]) or not (dp[i-1][j]). To break the circle, run this twice: once on slices[1..3n-1] (first excluded) and once on slices[0..3n-2] (last excluded); any valid circular selection avoids at least one endpoint, so the answer is covered. Each pass is O(m·n) time and can be compressed to O(n) space with rolling arrays.
s: Define solve(arr, k): max sum choosing k non-adjacent elements from linear array arr.
dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i-2][j-1] + arr[i]); initialize dp[i][0]=0, dp[-1][*]=0.
Run solve on slices without the first element, and on slices without the last element.
Return the maximum of the two runs.
a.t: O(n^2) — each of the two linear passes fills a table of size 3n × n.
a.sp: O(n^2) for the DP table; reducible to O(n) with rolling rows since dp[i] depends only on dp[i-1] and dp[i-2].

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, state the reduction first (exactly n picks, pairwise non-adjacent, circular), then present the two-pass linear DP as the main solution — it is simple, provably correct, and comfortably fast for n ≤ 500. The brute force is only worth mentioning briefly to motivate the DP.

Common pitfalls: forgetting the circularity (answering on the full array as if linear gives wrong results when both endpoints are picked); using a plain House-Robber recurrence that maximizes count rather than enforcing exactly n picks; and attempting a value-greedy/heap approach, which fails on inputs like `[8,9,8,6,1,1]`. Edge cases: minimum input of 3 slices (answer is just the single largest slice), and arrays where the optimal set includes neither endpoint.

Likely follow-ups: compress the DP to O(n) space with rolling arrays; reconstruct which slices are chosen; or generalize to picking k slices from a circular array of arbitrary length.
